title: The seventy-two (Luke 10:1–24)
hookLine: sent in pairs like lambs among wolves, peace to this house

lines: THE FIRST THING TO SAY AT A DOOR.
cards: Around the Epiphany in January, in some Catholic homes, someone climbs on a chair with a piece of blessed chalk and writes over the front door: the year, split in two, with three letters in the middle, C, M and B, joined by crosses.
People read the letters as the names tradition gives the three wise men, and also as the start of a Latin blessing: may Christ bless this house. It's a small, homemade custom.
The wish in it is much older: on a road in Luke, Jesus sends out a wider circle of disciples and tells them the first thing to say at every door.

teach.h: TWO AND TWO, BEFORE HIS FACE.
teach.b: Now he sends people ahead of him, and not just the twelve.
The Douay-Rheims says the Lord appointed "other seventy-two: and he sent them two and two before his face into every city and place whither he himself was to come." Two and two, so nobody goes alone.
Then the honest warning: "behold I send you as lambs among wolves." No purse, no bag, no sandals, no stopping to chat on the road.

And at every door, one sentence first: "Into whatsoever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house." If a son of peace is there, Jesus says, your peace will rest on him. If not, it will come back to you.
A blessing can't be wasted: it lands, or it returns. Behind the Gospel's word for peace stands the Hebrew shalom: not just quiet, but wholeness, everything as it should be.

The number is a small puzzle: some Bibles say seventy here, and the Douay says seventy-two. Some readers connect it with the list of the world's nations in Genesis chapter ten, and hear in it a message meant for everyone.
And the ending is pure joy. The seventy-two come back thrilled: even the devils obey us! Jesus says rejoice in something better: your names are written in heaven.

how: Some Catholic families bless their homes at Epiphany by chalking the year and the letters C+M+B over the door, and the traditional rite for blessing a house opens with Jesus' words, peace be to this house.

games.q: you're one of the seventy-two. you knock on a stranger's door in a town you've never seen. what do you say first?
o: ask if they'll let you stay.
games.why: Jesus tells them to say it first, before anything. if it isn't received, the peace comes back to them.

practice: Picture the next door you'll walk through: your own front door, an office, a classroom, a friend's apartment, a hospital room.
At the threshold, before you step in, wish peace on everyone inside, the ones you love and the ones you don't. If you pray, say his words silently: peace be to this house.

wordCard.voice: The seventy-two. The wider circle of disciples Jesus sent out two by two, as lambs among wolves, with peace as their first word at every door. Today's word.
